subject: research/qual-regression
professional: an applied statistician / computational social scientist who works on measurement error and prediction-powered inference (the DSL and PPI literature)

evidence.correctness: Ran `python3 research/qual-regression/experiments/run.py` (20 s): output equals experiments/results.txt except one trailing blank line, so every README table number reproduces. Recomputed independently with numpy (script not committed): (1) ols() coefficients and HC0 standard errors equal numpy lstsq plus a hand-built HC0 sandwich to 8 digits; (2) the naive E1 slope has a closed form, Cov(c,f)/Var(f) with p=0.3, sens=0.7, spec=0.95, giving 0.7379, against 0.740 in the README; (3) dsl() point estimates equal a separately written numpy solve of the inverse-probability-weighted estimating equation (identical to 8 digits on a seeded corpus); (4) class_shares_ppi() estimates and standard errors equal numpy one-vs-rest PPI to 15 digits. statsmodels was not installed, so HC0 was checked against numpy only. README arithmetic checked: 0.511/0.594 gives 14% narrower, 0.118/0.271 gives 56%, accuracy 0.3*.85+.4*.8+.3*.6 = 0.755. No wrong number found.
evidence.completeness: Claimed and checked: ols with HC0 (works), dsl for OLS with sandwich se (works, equals OLS for a perfect coder), class_shares_naive and class_shares_ppi (work), simulate and simulate_classes (work), E1, E2 and E3 tables (all reproduce), figure script and SVG present. Limitations section honestly lists what is not done (no logistic, no PPI++ power tuning, known constant pi only). No TODOs or stubs. research/PROJECTS.md line 1400 describes the milestone as 'DSL, PPI++' but PPI++ power tuning is not implemented (README says so).
evidence.verification: Ran `cd research/qual-regression && python3 -m unittest test_qualreg`: 5 tests, OK (1 s). Seeded three mutations in qualreg.py and reverted each with git checkout. (a) pi -> 1.5*pi in the dsl point-estimate correction: caught (test_dsl_unbiased_naive_attenuated failed). (b) sign flip of the PPI rectifier in class_shares_ppi: caught. (c) removed the 1/pi weight on the correction in the DSL influence rows, which corrupts the standard errors only: NOT caught, all 5 tests passed. No test checks any standard error from dsl or class_shares_ppi, or interval coverage, although coverage is the headline claim. The experiments are a check on coverage, but nothing runs in a test or CI.
evidence.craft: Read qualreg.py (168 lines), test_qualreg.py, experiments/run.py. Small, readable, stdlib only, docstrings explain the estimating equation, Gauss-Jordan solve with pivoting and a singular-system error. Defects: no input validation (pi outside (0,1], empty gold list, mismatched lengths give a ZeroDivisionError or silent nonsense); dsl() computes the outer products and residuals twice and the O(n) python loops are slow (20 s for the experiments); run.py docstring says 1-2 minutes while the README says about 15 s; E3 coverage is scored against each corpus's realised class share rather than the population share, which is not stated; the results are text, not machine-readable.
evidence.claims: Checked each headline claim against files: naive 0.74 and 0/300 coverage (results.txt E1), DSL 1.01 and 94% (E1), z coefficient 0.467 and 60% under correlated error (E2), 3-class shares off up to 8.5 points with 0% coverage and PPI 95.5-97% (E3). All back to results.txt. 'Every result is from simulated coders' and 'No real LLM was run' are stated in the first paragraph and in Limitations, with AI-assistance disclosure. Live page URL not loaded (no network check made). One soft claim: PROJECTS.md calls the milestone 'DSL, PPI++'.
evidence.fitness: Could a researcher build on it? Partly. The code is a clear, auditable reference for DSL-for-OLS, and the E2 point (a mismeasured regressor biases a perfectly measured covariate's coefficient) is a clean teaching example. But it is simulation only, with no real hand-coded corpus, no input API for a user's own CSV, no CLI, and the qualitative findings (naive attenuation, DSL restores coverage, small efficiency gain at 7% labels) are already shown in Egami et al. 2023 and the PPI papers. A researcher would use the DSL R package or the ppi_py package instead. The sweep over corpus size and coder quality that would make it informative is listed as next steps, not done.
evidence.domain: Nearest prior work: Egami et al. 2023 (DSL, with the official R package), Angelopoulos et al. 2023 and PPI++ (ppi_py), and the classical misclassification literature (Bound-Brown-Mathiowetz; Carroll et al.; Hausman et al. 1998). Method choices agree with DSL for OLS with known sampling probability and HC0 sandwich se, and the estimator was verified to match an independent implementation. A reviewer would object that (1) there is no comparison against the reference DSL package, only against a re-derivation by the same convention; (2) the error model is independent given the true code, which the README acknowledges; (3) finite-sample HC0 under-covers slightly (E1 DSL 0.937 on 300 studies, within noise); (4) the novelty over the cited papers is not stated, and the paper-level claim would need a real corpus.

defects.what: No test checks dsl() standard errors or coverage; a seeded mutation that removes the 1/pi weight in the influence rows passed all 5 tests, yet coverage is the headline claim

No comparison against the reference DSL (R) or ppi_py implementations and no statement of what is new relative to Egami et al. 2023; a statistician cannot tell whether this adds anything beyond a reimplementation
Simulation only and no user-facing interface for real data (no CSV or CLI entry point)
No input validation (pi range, empty gold set, length mismatches)
run.py docstring says 1-2 minutes, README says about 15 s, measured 20 s
E3 coverage is scored against each realised corpus share, not the population share, and the README does not say so
PROJECTS.md milestone says 'DSL, PPI++' but PPI++ power tuning is not implemented

verdict: Numerically sound and honestly scoped: every README number reproduces in 20 s, and four outputs (OLS and HC0 se, the naive-slope closed form 0.738 against 0.740, DSL point estimates, PPI shares and se) match independent numpy computation. It does not meet the bar because verification is 2: the tests catch bias bugs but a mutation that corrupts the DSL standard errors, which drive the headline coverage claim, passes all tests. As research it is a clear teaching-grade reimplementation of published methods on simulated data, with no real corpus, no comparison to the reference packages and no stated novelty, so fitness and domain are 2.
